# Didache Chapter 9 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Hierosolymitanus (H), Didache 9

---

## Chapter 9

**1** Concerning the Eucharist, give thanks in the following manner.

**2** First, over the cup:

> We give you thanks, our Father,
> for the holy vine of David your servant,
> which you have made known to us through Jesus your servant.
> To you be glory forever.

**3** Then over the broken bread:

> We give you thanks, our Father,
> for the life and knowledge
> which you have made known to us through Jesus your servant.
> To you be glory forever.

**4** As this broken bread was scattered upon the mountains and, being gathered together, became one — so let your Church be gathered together from the ends of the earth into your kingdom;

**5** for yours is the glory and the power through Jesus Christ forever.

No one is to eat or drink of your Eucharist except those who have been baptized in the name of the Lord — for the Lord himself has said regarding this: "Do not give what is holy to the dogs."

---

### Council Notes

**On παῖς — "servant" vs. "child":** The Greek παῖς means both "servant" and "child." In the context of the Servant Songs of Isaiah (LXX uses παῖς for עֶבֶד in Isa 52:13), "servant" is the primary meaning. But "child of God" is also present. All agents use "servant"; SOPHIA agrees. A translator note should preserve the double resonance.

**On the cup-before-bread sequence:** All agents preserve this order, which is attested only here in early Christian literature (Paul gives bread then cup in 1 Cor 11). This may reflect a meal structure where the cup of blessing preceded the bread, or a distinct liturgical tradition. It is historically significant and must not be reordered.

**On v.4 — the scattered bread image:** This is the most celebrated passage in the Didache and one of the most beautiful images in early Christian literature. All agents render it faithfully. PNEUMA's expansion ("grain growing on hillside after hillside") adds vivid imagery not in the Greek. SOPHIA retains the concise Greek form: "scattered upon the mountains... gathered together... became one." The starkness of the image is its power.

**On v.5 — restriction to the baptized:** All agents agree: "Do not give what is holy to the dogs" cites Matthew 7:6 and grounds the communion restriction in the Lord's own teaching. The exclusion of the unbaptized from the Eucharist is here presented as a dominical command, not merely a community rule.

**On "Eucharist" vs. "thanksgiving":** SOPHIA retains "Eucharist" as the technical liturgical term. The Didache itself uses it as a technical term for the rite (not merely "thanksgiving" in the generic sense). The ritual and the term were already bound together.
